text: The assembly will hear addressed by his
excellency Yamandu Orsi, president of
the Oriental Republic of Uruguay. I
request protocol to escort his
excellency and invite him to address the
assembly.
Mr. President of the General Assembly,
Mr. Secretary General,
Heads of State,
ladies and gentlemen,
it is fitting that I begin by paying
tribute to the people of the United
States who 250 years ago, a quarter of a
millennium ago, decided and understood
that people have rights, the right to
life, to their liberty, and to happiness
and that these rights should guide every
government and that it is the governed
who should decide who should govern
them. We in South America
also peoples of migrants
inherited these same principles 50 years
on and to that we say cheers.
I appear before this assembly on behalf
of a young country, but one with deeply
rooted traditions. A country that over
the course of its history has learned
that governing doesn't merely mean
administering resources or institutions.
Above all, it means working for the
well-being of people.
And that has been one of Uruguay's great
purposes, building a society in which
dignity, freedom,
peaceful coexistence and opportunities
can be a part of people's everyday
lives. And if there is one word that
sums up much of our vocation as a
country, that word would be peace.
We do not view peace simply as an
absence of war. We understand it as
something that has to be constantly
built. The possibility for people to
live, to work, to educate their
children, pursue their aspirations, and
to look to the future without fear.
Uruguay
>> with its virtues, but also like every
country with its darker times has been a
country that has sought to resolve its
differences through institutions,
through dialogue, and through the quest
for agreement.
In this assembly, we reaffirm our
enduring willingness to contribute to
peacekeeping missions with a deep sense
of responsibility and solidarity.
Uruguan men and women can bear witness
to the value of this instrument in
easing suffering and guaranteeing
respect for the human lives of the most
defenseless populations. You can
continue to count on Uruguay here. We
are not a country given to grand
gestures. We are a country of deeply
held beliefs. And one of these beliefs
is that peaceuilding is never finished.
We can't take it for granted. Every
generation has the responsibility
to build it a new. There can't be peace
for some and another peace for others.
No suffering matters more because it
happens closer to home. And no lives are
worth less because they were born in
another country.
When people suffer, humanity as a whole
bears a responsibility. When a people is
displaced, when a family loses its home,
when young people can see no way out and
their mental health is under threat,
when a child grows up under the sound of
gunfire, when millions of people live in
poverty or without any opportunities, we
can't stand indifferent to that.
Nor can we stand indifferent to the pain
caused by a state of endless war, the
fear and pain generated by organized
crime or the constant threat of
terrorism, the repression borne out of
tyranny or the suffering
triggered by a rigid economic blockade
such as that endured by the Cuban
people.
We don't believe that taking one side or
another in a war, confrontation or
dispute necessarily contributes to
resolving it.
Indeed, very often it only serves to
further the divisions.
We have a different commitment that is
to seek paths towards understanding to
open spaces for dialogue and to help to
ensure that conflicts find a peaceful
resolution.
This doesn't mean indifference. It
doesn't mean downplaying suffering. It
doesn't mean overlooking
responsibilities.
It means understanding that peace
demands something more difficult than
merely taking sides. It means that we
need to work so that that confrontation
can be brought to an end as soon as
possible. And to do that, we also have
to recover something that at times seems
to have been lost in international
debate. Humility.
Uruguayans have an expression that sums
up an understanding of coexistence. No
one is better than anyone else. No
country holds the absolute truth. No
nation has a monopoly on their
solutions. No society can claim that its
historical experience is universal and
no people
should be doomed to choose between
models imposed from outside.
Our understanding of relations among
countries stems from that notion of
humility.
This is a humility that doesn't mean
weakness. On the contrary, it means
recognizing our own limitations while at
the same time trusting in the abilities
of others. We come from a country that
is diverse in its opinions, but one that
is deeply committed to the possibility
of building a common future.
And we believe that this combination,
diversity of ideas and cohesion around
the future, can also serve as our
contribution to the international
community.
Today we are living through a
particularly difficult period. Extreme
inequality remains one of the great
threats to coexistence. Poverty
continues to deprive millions of people
of basic opportunities and wars continue
to destroy lives, communities and hopes.
While we discuss growth, technology,
artificial intelligence, the energy
transition, or new forms of production,
there are millions of people who
continue to ask themselves far more
basic questions.
How will I feed my children? How can I
find housing? How can I find a job? Or
how can I face tomorrow without fear?
We mustn't lose sight of that reality.
Development makes sense when it improves
people's lives.
Economies make sense when they serve
society. Technology makes sense when it
expands our freedoms and opportunities.
And politics makes sense when it is able
to transform reality
to bring happiness to our people.
We are speaking from the experience of a
small country removed from the great
centers of power. However, we're
convinced that our size shouldn't
determine our ability to contribute,
much less affect our own dignity.
We need more effective, more
representative, multilateral
institutions that are closer to the
people and more able to respond to the
challenges of our time. We need
cooperation. We need solidarity
and we also need to demonstrate
austerity within these institutions. But
above all, we need to restore trust in
our collective ability to change things.
Because
at its heart, the very idea of
well-being and progress springs from
something that is profoundly human. That
is the ability to recognize suffering
and refuse to accept inertia.
Human beings are creative precisely
because they refuse to resign themselves
to things. They sense what causes pain.
They sense what could be different. And
then they're able to sense the desire
for change. And this desire for change
is perhaps one of the most profound
expressions of our own freedom. When our
peoples advance along the path of
progress, they generally do so by
wielding the powerful magic of freedom.
Knowing that freedom doesn't com involve
solely choosing between different
possibilities. It also means having
being able to transform those things
that we wish to for the good of the
community as a whole. Our freedom
becomes fuller when we are able to
expand the freedom of others. When we
change our societies through dialogue.
When we build more when we build fairer
institutions. When we undertake
significant projects that endure beyond
our own lifetimes. When school a new
school opens its doors. When a child has
an opportunity that was previously out
of their reach. When a community is able
to overcome a division. When two
countries that were at odds finally find
a path towards understanding.
Today there are more than 8 billion
people living on the same planet.
8 billion different stories, 8 billion
hopes,
8 billion possibilities.
We're not finished as such as humanity.
We are a humanity still in the making.
Every morning, we have the chance to
decide what kind of world we want to
leave to those who come after us. We can
choose to accept inequality as
inevitable. We could accept war as
something permanent, accept poverty as
our fate. We could accept mistrust
replacing dialogue. Or on the contrary,
we could choose another path,
the most difficult path, but also the
most human one. Uruguay therefore comes
before this assembly today with that
belief with the humility and respect of
a small country but also with the
resolve of those who understand the
value of their principles. We've come to
say that peace is no utopia. It is an
ongoing endeavor.
No conflict is ever definitively
resolved through more conflict. No
society becomes safer when hopelessness
becomes the norm. No country can build
its well-being in isolation.
The future of humanity will to a large
extent depend on our ability to
understand that we are profoundly
interconnected. We are different. We
think differently. We have different
histories. We have different interests.
We are well aware that this isn't a
struggle between the good guys and the
bad guys.
All too often, the good guys quickly
become the bad guys, or those that we
harshly condemned yesterday magically
become the standardbearers of our
alliance for good. But we share the same
planet and ultimately the same destiny.
Every day the UN has an increasing
reason to exist and it must inevitably
evolve in step with the geopolitical
changes unfolding at dizzying speed.
Every nation within this organization
must play an active role within it each
to the fullest extent of their
capacities.
It's clear that our efforts should focus
on ensuring that this is an upto-date
organization properly supported taking
fair decisions that are respected.
Countries borders cannot be subject to
human whims. They must be protected and
respected as they represent the
boundaries established to preserve
identity, distinctive character and a
sense of belonging of their respective
populations. We cannot continue to be
held hostage to the will of a handful of
countries that can be counted on the
fingers of one hand.
Nor can we yield to the economic
expediencies of the time. The aim here
is clear. to achieve lasting stability,
to ensure that the efforts of our
citizens and their governments are
channeled towards generating prosperity,
far removed, of course, from the
destruction and suffering caused by war.
And we have made a commitment. Let us
honor it right now. The history that
ultimately prevails will be the history
that we write every day through our
action. For all of these reasons,
Uruguay will continue to support
dialogue, multilateralism, cooperation,
international law,
and the peaceful settlement of disputes,
and above all
for the dignity of every human being.
Humanity continues to refuse to regard
itself as definitively complete. And
perhaps that's our greatest hope. The
hope that we can still change, that we
can still learn,
that we can still build, and that we can
still choose peace.
And this mere fact ultimately reminds us
of the clear purity of the idea that
together we stand and together we
change.
Little is contributed to the purposes of
the UN by merely using this rostrm to
accuse or attack
fire. The fire doesn't need any more
fuel. Let us better harness this
opportunity and let us give peace
another chance because relations among
states
just like relations between good people
bring happiness.
if we refrain from trading blows or
elbowing one another aside. Thank you
very much.
